aboutRight.aboutText: A forward deployed engineer is the person sent into the customer's building to turn a product into a working, defensible outcome: install it in their environment, configure it to their process, build the reporting their people will actually use, train the team, and stay accountable after go-live. I was doing that job before it had the title. At Nasdaq BWise I implemented a governance, risk and compliance platform onsite for banks, insurers and corporates. Every client meant adapting not just to their data but to their business: learning how that company saw its own risks before touching a control library, managing expectations in the room and after I had rolled off, and delivering under real pressure on a justifiable, timely basis rather than stamping a deliverable and leaving. I was the business intelligence lead by title, but I looked at what the customer was getting from the whole platform they had bought, and went beyond my slice of it, because the measure of the work was whether they asked to work with me again. Then six years inside one bank, MUFG, and later Citi: twelve years in enterprise data, a decade of it across banks, building platforms that lived under audit. Touring many companies teaches you patterns; staying in one industry teaches you why the pattern does not apply here. Today the product is AI: agents, retrieval, governed pipelines. The job is the same. Decompose the vague brief, ship inside your change control, leave an audit trail your examiner can read, and own it after it is live.

archivement.text: Platforms on Snowflake, Databricks, Azure and AWS, built for teams whose outputs go to regulators, auditors and clients.
Six years at MUFG, then Citi, plus Nomura and the GRC vendor side at Nasdaq BWise. Logos below are employers and client organisations I delivered for.

experienceData.text: Computer Science from the New York Institute of Technology (Phi Eta Sigma National Honor) and an MBA with a Chartered Financial Analyst concentration from Quinnipiac University (Magna Cum Laude). Currently completing a Master of Science in Artificial Intelligence and the Anthropic Claude certification. The technical half builds the system; the finance half is why I can sit with a CFO, a risk officer or an examiner and speak their language about what the system does.

serviceData.title: Discovery: turn the vague brief into workstreams
serviceData.heading: Week 0 to 1
serviceData.text: Every engagement starts with a room: the sponsor, the people who run the process today, and whoever has to sign off. I leave with a written scope: the system of record, the constraint (change control, data residency, a regulator, a legacy platform), success criteria in numbers, and a decomposition into workstreams you can staff and track. That document is the contract for everything after it.

serviceData.title: Build inside your environment, not next to it
serviceData.heading: Weeks 1 to N
serviceData.text: The code runs on your infrastructure, under your identity provider, through your release process. Python and TypeScript, MCP connectors into core systems with authentication, data mapping, error handling and audit requirements built in, retrieval over your own documents, agents where an agent is the right tool and plain pipelines where it is not. Small releases, days rather than quarters.

serviceData.title: Production with an audit trail
serviceData.heading: Go-live
serviceData.text: Before anything touches a real workflow: output validation, evaluation sets, lineage, logging, model-risk controls a second-line reviewer can read. If an examiner asks what the system did on a given day, the answer is a record, not a memory. This is the habit I brought from six years at MUFG and it is the part most AI deployments skip.

serviceData.title: Handover and ownership after go-live
serviceData.heading: After launch
serviceData.text: You keep what I build: repos, runbooks, evaluation harnesses, the trained team. I stay on the hook for the outcome, not the demo: monitoring, tuning, the year-two story. Engagement shapes: embedded contract, fixed-scope build, or a forward deployed role inside your organisation. Onsite, embedded or remote, in the US and with clients abroad.

portfolioData.subTitle: Nasdaq BWise · governance, risk and compliance · forward deployed
portfolioData.title: GRC platform implementations, onsite, for regulated clients

paragraphList.text:
Situation
Nasdaq BWise sold a governance, risk and compliance platform (risk management, regulatory compliance, internal controls, internal audit, information security) to banks, insurers and corporates. Selling it was the easy half. Each client needed it installed in their environment, configured to their own control framework and risk taxonomy, reporting built for their board and their regulator, and a team trained to run it without us.

Constraint
Client environments, client change control, client auditors. A risk taxonomy is an argument about how a company sees itself, and three functions rarely agree on it. Every configuration decision had to be defensible to a second-line risk function, and every report had to answer a real question rather than look clean.

What shipped
Onsite installation and configuration; the control library and risk hierarchy loaded and versioned; dashboards and management reporting for boards, risk committees and regulators; data migration from spreadsheet registers; user and administrator training; hypercare with exit criteria; and the pre-sales scoping that turned one implementation into the next.

Time to production
Phased: a working screen against the client's own data early, then configuration, migration and reporting in increments the steering committee could see every week. What you discover onsite is different from what was sold, so discovery was re-run in the building even when a signed scope already existed.

Outcome
Clients who asked to work with me again. That was the metric I ran on. A platform their own people operated after I rolled off, reporting that assembled itself instead of being rebuilt by hand each cycle, and a shared risk language across functions that had not had one.

What broke, and the fix
The recurring failure in GRC work is not technical: evidence that never arrives from control owners, approvals stuck with Legal, remediation nobody tracks until the auditor asks. My counter-move was to look past my own reporting scope, design the workflow around the control owner's actual week, price every new request in time and money at the moment it was made, and measure adoption as a go-live criterion. Bedside manner is technique: ask what they think the answer is, and when you overrule it, explain why in their language.

portfolioData.subTitle: MUFG · investment banking · then Citi
portfolioData.title: Six years inside one bank: enterprise data under audit

paragraphList.text:
Situation
After years of moving between clients, six years in one place: the investment banking data organisation at MUFG, followed by Citi. The work was enterprise data platforms, business intelligence and data engineering for teams whose outputs went to regulators, auditors and the front office.

Constraint
Bank change control, model risk, internal and external audit. Systems that live under audit acquire habits: append-only logs, lineage, reconciliations that explain themselves, evidence that survives hostile review. A release that cannot show its test plan and its rollback does not ship.

What shipped
Data platforms and reporting that were built to the release process rather than around it: small increments that passed review, documented controls, and reporting cycles that ran without a person rebuilding them. And a depth of domain knowledge that only staying buys: how the business actually makes and loses money, and why the generic pattern does not apply here.

Time to production
Continuous over six years, in weekly and monthly increments inside the bank's release calendar, rather than one big-bang delivery.

Outcome
The judgment I bring into every AI deployment now: what a second-line reviewer will ask, what an examiner accepts as evidence, and how to ship inside a bank without fighting its change control. Twelve years in enterprise data, a decade across banks.

What broke, and the fix
Consultants and employees are both expendable; that is the honest part of both careers. The lesson was to leave systems that run without you and still be the person they call back. Designing the exit from the start, and writing the handover while you are still in the room, is how you do both.

portfolioData.subTitle: Own product · self-hosted · redaction, policy as code, hash-chained audit log
portfolioData.title: Ledgerproof: a governed AI gateway for accounting firms

paragraphList.text:
Situation
Small US tax and accounting firms are financial institutions under the FTC Safeguards Rule, and the IRS Office of Professional Responsibility now expects documented review of AI output. Staff were already pasting client data into public chatbots with no record of what left.

Constraint
Nothing may route through a vendor. The control has to run on the firm's own machine, work with OpenAI, Anthropic or a fully local model, and produce evidence an examiner accepts.

What shipped
A self-hosted gateway: PII and tax-data redaction before any prompt leaves (Presidio plus tax-tuned rules), YAML policy enforced as running code (allow, redact, block per data class), a hash-chained tamper-evident audit log, a one-click examiner-ready Evidence Pack, a Claude Desktop MCP mode, Docker and Windows installers. 50 tests green on every build.

Time to production
Built and shipped as a product in one continuous build, then reshaped after research. Installs in about two weeks per firm.

Outcome
Pilot stage. A healthcare pilot on synthetic patient data is in build: a HIPAA policy profile covering the Safe Harbor identifiers, and three generative deliverables (imaging report narrative, patient communication, patient-management brief) that run through the gateway and are handed to the client's own developers as production code. No real patient data is used at any stage.

What broke, and the fix
The first version led with the firewall. Research showed redaction is now table stakes inside the tools firms already buy; the thing nobody else produces is the evidence. The product and the pitch were reshaped around the Evidence Pack.

portfolioData.subTitle: Own practice · architecture for local models and agents
portfolioData.title: Orchest AI: the self-hosted agent stack you own

paragraphList.text:
Situation
Open-weight models reached parity on code, yet enterprise open-source share fell from 19% to 11% in a year. Not a capability gap: nobody knows how to architect and operate the stack.

Constraint
The client owns the hardware, the weights, the harness and the data. The architect designs it, proves it, hands it over, and does not become a dependency.

What shipped
Reference architecture: OpenClaw-style agent harness, Ollama or vLLM serving, a 27B to 32B open model with 64K context as the floor, retrieval over the client's documents, approval gates and spend caps, an operating loop (plan, apply, unify, loop) with observability. Plus the honest limits page: where a frontier API is still the right call.

Time to production
Engagements start with a two-week written Architecture Review, then a 90-day build sequence the client can run with or without me.

Outcome
An ownership manifest, a published reference stack, and a retainer scoped on outcomes rather than hours. The client keeps the weights, the infra, the prompts, the evals and the repo.

What broke, and the fix
The first site sold eight generic skills and a Calendly. Rebuilt around the ownership manifest and the reference stack, because a vendor can list features and only an architect can list what you keep.

portfolioData.subTitle: AI & Data Analytics · YouTube × Amazon Prime
portfolioData.title: Beast Games Content Intelligence Platform

paragraphList.text:
Overview
Collaborated on a full-stack data analytics platform built around MrBeast's Beast Games - the largest reality competition in YouTube history, which crossed 8.5M viewers on Amazon Prime for its Season 2 premiere. The project decodes the content strategy patterns driving viewership and engagement across MrBeast's multi-channel network (471M, 40M, and 26M subscribers), turning creative intuition into measurable, repeatable performance signals.

What Was Built
An interactive 9-tab Streamlit analytics dashboard covering: channel metrics, platform breakdowns, title optimization analysis, episode structure and retention curves, celebrity guest impact modeling, upload timing patterns, a content opportunity prediction matrix, and a fan engagement intelligence layer called BeastBet - an audience prediction system that connects analytics outputs directly back to production workflows.

Key Findings
• Titles of 6-9 words achieve the highest click-through rates; including prize amounts correlates with a ~31% CTR lift
• Thursday-Saturday uploads generate ~18% more Day-1 views
• Red/high-contrast thumbnails outperform muted designs by ~22%
• A critical 34% audience drop-off occurs at the 14-16 minute mark - a direct signal for episode pacing decisions
• Celebrity guest episodes average a 2.1× viewership multiplier

Tech Stack & Integration
Built in Python using pandas, NumPy, Plotly, scikit-learn, and SciPy for analysis and modeling. The front-end dashboard runs on Streamlit. Data is sourced live via the YouTube Data API v3 and supplemented with Amazon Prime viewership metrics, managed through a YAML-based channel data store. A/B testing and anomaly detection modules (ab_testing.py, anomaly_detection.py) power the statistical rigor behind each recommendation.

portfolioData.subTitle: Power BI · AI Strategy · Model Routing
portfolioData.title: Enterprise AI Cost Optimization Dashboard

paragraphList.text:
Overview
A Power BI executive dashboard designed to visualize and optimize enterprise AI infrastructure spend. The dashboard provides real-time visibility into AI costs across model tiers, use cases, and business units, enabling data-driven decisions about where to invest, where to cut, and how to maximize ROI on AI initiatives.

Key Features
• Model Routing Analysis - Visualizes request distribution across model tiers (frontier vs. mid-tier vs. lightweight), identifying opportunities to route 60-70% of simple tasks to cheaper models
• Cost-Per-Inference Tracking - Breaks down spend by department, use case, and model
• Cache Hit Rate Monitoring - Measures semantic deduplication effectiveness and projects savings
• Savings Simulator - Interactive what-if analysis showing projected cost reduction from implementing optimization strategies

Business Impact
The framework demonstrates how enterprises can reduce AI infrastructure costs by 40%+ through intelligent model routing, tiered inference architecture, and governance-first design - without sacrificing model quality or response time.

Tech Stack
Built with Power BI (DAX, Power Query), connected to AI usage telemetry via Azure Monitor and REST APIs. Data modeling follows a star schema optimized for cost attribution across organizational hierarchies.

blogData.title: The onsite implementation playbook: what years across GRC clients and six years inside one bank taught me

paragraphList.text: My first week onsite at a bank, the signed scope and the actual problem were two different documents. That is not a failure of the sales process. It is the job. What you discover in the building is always different from what was sold, and the implementation consultant is the person hired to close that gap without anyone losing face.

The vendor's view and the customer's view of the same platform are different products. At Nasdaq BWise I implemented a governance, risk and compliance platform for banks, insurers and corporates, and every client meant adapting to their business before their data. A risk taxonomy is an argument about how a company sees itself. Three functions will not agree on it, and you configure against a versioned first draft while the argument continues, or the project stalls in workshops.

Managing expectations is a delivery skill, not a soft skill. Every new request gets priced in time and money at the moment it is asked, in the room, not at the end of the phase. New requests were never the problem. Silent ones were. A weekly cadence that shows accomplishments, next milestones, risks and budget keeps a steering committee from ever being surprised, and a committee that is never surprised keeps signing.

Bedside manner is technique. I was the business intelligence lead by title, and the reporting layer could be perfect while the customer still did not get what they bought, because the evidence never arrived from the control owners, approvals sat with Legal, and remediation went untracked until the auditor asked. Looking past your own scope at what they are getting from the whole product is how you earn the second engagement. Ask what they think the answer is. When you overrule it, explain why in their language, so the disagreement stays about the work.

Onsite and after you roll off are different jobs. In the room you can show a working screen on day two and settle a week of debate in ten minutes. After you leave, only what you wrote down and what you made their people run in front of you survives. So the handover gets written while you are still onsite, hypercare ends on exit criteria rather than a calendar date, and the exit is designed at the start.

Then I stopped touring. Six years in one bank, MUFG, and later Citi. Touring twelve clients teaches you patterns. Staying teaches you why the pattern does not apply here: how the business actually makes and loses money, what a second-line reviewer will ask, what an examiner accepts as evidence. Each half of the career made the other half worth more.

The honest part: consultants and employees are both expendable. The only answer I have found is to leave systems that run without you and to be the person they call back anyway. That is the whole playbook, and it is the same playbook I use now when the product being installed is AI.

blogData.title: What a forward deployed engineer actually does, and why the title is newer than the job

paragraphList.text: The title showed up on job boards in volume this year: postings went from a few hundred to over five thousand in twelve months. The job did not. Anyone who has implemented a governance platform onsite for a bank already knows it: you write production code, you deploy it inside the customer's environment, and you own the outcome after the contract is signed.

Three things separate it from consulting. You ship, you do not advise and leave. You work inside the customer's change control instead of around it. And you carry the outcome into year two: monitoring, evaluation, the quiet fixes nobody writes a case study about.

The skill hiring managers say they test most is decomposition: take a vague, slightly frightening brief and turn it into workstreams a team can staff. The second is comfort with a room that has a C-suite sponsor and a line analyst in it at the same time. The technical bar is table stakes.
If you are hiring for it, ask for the discovery document from a past deployment, not the demo. If you are becoming one, publish yours.

blogData.title: Change control is not the enemy: shipping AI inside a bank's release process

paragraphList.text: Most AI pilots die at the same gate. The demo worked in a sandbox; the release process asks for evidence, rollback, access review and a named owner, and the team that built the demo has none of it.

The fix is not to fight change control. It is to build to it from day one: environment parity, a written test plan, evaluation sets that a second-line reviewer can rerun, logging that answers what the system did on a given date, and a rollback that is a command rather than a meeting.

Small releases matter more in regulated environments, not less. A weekly increment that passes review beats a quarterly big bang that sits in a queue. Days rather than quarters is achievable inside a bank; it just has to be designed for.

The version of this I learned at MUFG: a release that could not show its test plan and its rollback did not ship, and the teams who resented that spent their quarters in the queue. The teams who built to it shipped weekly. Change control was never the constraint. Building as if it did not exist was.

blogData.title: The audit trail is the product: evidence-first AI for regulated firms

paragraphList.text: Every vendor in the AI governance space sells a control: redaction, filtering, policy. Almost nobody sells the thing the examiner actually asks for, which is proof. The auditor's favourite question has not changed: show me where your policy says X, then show me the evidence you are actually doing X.

In June the IRS Office of Professional Responsibility applied Circular 230 to AI use and said, in plain terms, that documentation of the review of AI output is expected. That is a federal regulator naming an artifact.

Building Ledgerproof taught me the order of operations. The gateway, the redaction and the policy engine are necessary. The hash-chained log and the Evidence Pack are what a firm owner can hand to whoever is asking. Lead with the proof; the control is the reason the proof can be trusted.
The same logic applies to any AI system in a bank, an insurer or a clinic. If the record does not exist, the control did not happen.

blogData.title: Own your AI: why open-weight parity did not move enterprise adoption

paragraphList.text: Open-weight models caught up on code this year. Enterprise share of open-source models fell anyway, from 19% to 11%. The capability arrived; the adoption went the other way.

The reason is not the models. Running a 27B to 32B model with a 64K context window on hardware you own, serving it reliably, wiring an agent harness to it, and operating the result under your own security controls is an architecture and operations problem. Very few teams have done it once.

The economics are real: a self-hosted model on an entry server pays for itself in months at moderate volume, and for firms with data that cannot leave the building the cloud option was never really available. What is missing is the person who designs the stack, proves it, and hands it over without becoming a dependency.
That is the practice I run at Orchest AI. The site lists the reference stack, the ownership manifest, and the honest limits page, including where a frontier API is still the right answer.

blogData.title: Agents are not the default: loops, harnesses, and when a plain pipeline wins

paragraphList.text: The question I get most from operators now is not whether to use agents. It is what they actually get from agentic adoption, and what to do when an agent is the wrong tool.

Three shapes cover most real work. A pipeline: deterministic steps, a model inside one or two of them, no autonomy, easiest to audit. A loop: a recurring goal with memory that runs on a schedule, checks what changed, acts, and pauses at a guardrail for a human. An agent: open-ended planning over tools, which you reserve for problems where the path genuinely cannot be written down in advance.

Harness engineering is the discipline around all three: the context each step sees, what gets logged, how work is delegated to sub-agents, how sessions are compacted and handed off, where spend caps and approval gates sit. It is not a trend. It is what makes any of the three survive contact with a real workflow.

Start with the pipeline. Promote to a loop when the job recurs. Promote to an agent only when you have evidence the path cannot be fixed. Most teams that skipped those steps are now paying for it in tokens and trust.
